Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.
Figure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens.

We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers.
Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup.
In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra.
That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts.

The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra — a fraction of the power used by a common toaster.
Figure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra.

We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half.

Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than…
